data.title: Dapsone (oral + topical gel)
data.summary: Antileprosy drugs · Sulfone (4,4'-diaminodiphenyl sulfone); antibacterial and anti-inflammatory
data.body:
_More from Khopkar · Antileprosy drugs_

**Class:** Sulfone (4,4'-diaminodiphenyl sulfone); antibacterial and anti-inflammatory

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial: like sulfonamides, competes with PABA and inhibits dihydropteroate synthase → no folate synthesis in M. leprae (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase and the halide–peroxide system → less oxidative tissue damage
- Also inhibits neutrophil adherence (integrin-mediated) and chemotaxis, and eosinophil peroxidase
- Hence its value in neutrophil-predominant dermatoses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; half-life about 24–30 h (once daily)
- Metabolised by N-acetylation (fast/slow acetylators) and N-hydroxylation (CYP2C9, 3A4) → hydroxylamine metabolite causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia
- Enterohepatic circulation; excreted in urine

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Leprosy (part of MDT)
- Dermatitis herpetiformis (drug of choice — itch improves within 48–72 h)
- Linear IgA disease, bullous SLE, subcorneal pustular dermatosis, erythema elevatum diutinum, mucous membrane pemphigoid, bullous pemphigoid (adjunct), IgA pemphigus
- Neutrophilic and vasculitic: urticarial vasculitis, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet disease
- Others: chronic urticaria (refractory), granuloma faciale, actinomycetoma (Welsh regimen with co-trimoxazole), loxoscelism, relapsing polychondritis, acne (topical)

## Dose & formulations
- Leprosy: 100 mg daily (adults), 1–2 mg/kg in children
- Dermatoses: start 25–50 mg/day, increase by 25–50 mg weekly to 100–200 mg/day (max usually 300 mg); taper to the lowest effective dose
- Check G6PD before starting
- Tablets 25, 50, 100 mg

## Adverse effects
- Dose-related haemolysis (in everyone; Hb falls 1–2 g/dL) — severe in G6PD deficiency
- Methaemoglobinaemia (dose-related): grey-blue lips, breathlessness, headache; usually tolerated below 10–12%; cimetidine or vitamin E may reduce it; methylene blue for severe cases (not in G6PD deficiency)
- Agranulocytosis (idiosyncratic, usually in the first 3 months) — sore throat, fever
- Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS-like): 2–8 weeks after starting — fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis; linked to HLA-B*13:01 (common in Asians); can be fatal
- Hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice; peripheral motor neuropathy (distal weakness); psychosis
- Exfoliative dermatitis, TEN, fixed drug eruption

## Contraindications
- Severe G6PD deficiency; previous dapsone hypersensitivity
- Caution: anaemia, cardiopulmonary disease (cannot tolerate methaemoglobinaemia), sulfonamide allergy (cross-reactivity uncommon)

## Drug interactions
- Trimethoprim raises dapsone levels (and vice versa) → more methaemoglobinaemia
- Rifampicin lowers dapsone levels (about 7–10 times) — not clinically important in MDT
- Probenecid raises levels; other oxidant drugs (primaquine, nitrates, EMLA/prilocaine) add to methaemoglobinaemia
- Cimetidine reduces hydroxylamine formation (used to lower methaemoglobin)

## Monitoring
- Baseline: G6PD, CBC, LFT, renal function, urine; HLA-B*13:01 where available
- CBC weekly for 4 weeks, every 2 weeks until 12 weeks, then every 3–4 months; LFT periodically; methaemoglobin if symptomatic
- Ask about fever, rash, sore throat and weakness at each visit

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for leprosy (WHO); risk of neonatal haemolysis and hyperbilirubinaemia near term. Excreted in milk — watch for haemolysis in G6PD-deficient infants.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis
- Haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia are dose-related; agranulocytosis and hypersensitivity syndrome are idiosyncratic
- Check G6PD first; HLA-B*13:01 for dapsone hypersensitivity
- Mechanism in skin: inhibits neutrophil myeloperoxidase

## Topical form: Dapsone gel (5%, 7.5%)
_Topical sulfone in a gel vehicle_

**Mechanism**
- Anti-inflammatory (neutrophil myeloperoxidase inhibition) and antibacterial against C. acnes

**Indications**
- Acne vulgaris (inflammatory, especially in adult women); rosacea (off-label)

**Dose & how to apply**
- 5% gel twice daily or 7.5% gel once daily

**Adverse effects**
- Dryness, redness; temporary orange-brown discolouration if used with benzoyl peroxide
- Blood levels are about 100 times lower than with oral dapsone — no routine G6PD test needed

**Contraindications**
- Hypersensitivity

**Pregnancy:** Limited data; minimal absorption.

**Viva points**
- Topical dapsone + BPO → orange skin staining

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.20 (Dapsone); Khopkar ch.6 (Antileprosy drugs); Wolverton 4e ch.20 and ch.46 (topical dapsone). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
